### To Reproduce

We are using below config where the first one is for latin characters in english and the second one is for arabic characters.

```
import localFont from 'next/font/local';

export const myProxima = localFont({
  variable: '--my-proxima',
  display: 'swap',
  adjustFontFallback: false,
  src: [
    {
      path: './Proxima-Nova-Bold.woff2',
      weight: '700',

    },
    {

    },

      weight: '400',
      style: 'italic',
    },

      weight: '400',
      style: 'normal',
    },
    {
      path: './Proxima-Nova-Semibold.woff2',
      weight: '600',
      style: 'normal',
    },
    {
      path: './Proxima-Nova-Thin-Italic.woff2',
      weight: '200',
      style: 'italic',
    },
    {
      path: './Proxima-Nova-Thin.woff2',
      weight: '200',
      style: 'normal',
    },
  ],
});

export const myGESS = localFont({
  variable: '--my-gess',
  display: 'swap',
  adjustFontFallback: false,
  src: [
    {
      path: './GESSTwoLight.woff',
      weight: '200',
      style: 'normal',
    },
    {
      path: './GESSTwoLight.woff',
      weight: '300',
      style: 'normal',
    },
    {
      path: './GESSTwoLight.woff',
      weight: '400',
      style: 'normal',
    },
    {
      path: './GESSTwoMedium.woff',
      weight: '600',
      style: 'normal',
    },
    {
      path: './GESSTwoBold.woff',
      weight: '700',
      style: 'normal',
    },
  ],
});

```

### Describe the Bug

Normally we can just rely on font-face to automatically switch the font to the one which is able to handle all characters in a displayed string.
After starting to use next/font we need to pass the prop `adjustFontFallback: true` as otherwise the english font would always over take the arabic font as the fallback will be always applied.
Similarly if we don't add it on arabic we would start displaying arabic numbers instead of latin numbers which in our use case is also unconventional.

For now we are handling it via adjustFontFallback but that defeats the purpose of improving our CLS.

Same issue was reported here but closed: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/44825

### Expected Behavior

Able to add a fallback which acts the same way as the font that was assigned so that we can handle such cases via normal font-face behavior of the browser to use the font-family which is able to handle all characters of string.

### Describe the Bug

My team stumbled upon this when they were configuring [Eslint](https://eslint.org). We decided to use the [quote-props](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/quote-props) rule with the following configuration:

```json
{
    "rules": [

    ]
}
```

The linter would instruct us to change the line like this (add quotes):

```diff

+ const inter = Inter({ 'subsets': 'latin' });
```

Which, when built, results in the error "Unexpected object key type". I tracked down the error in these two files:

[packages/next-swc/crates/next-font/src/font_imports_generator.rs](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next-swc/crates/next-font/src/font_imports_generator.rs#L197)
[packages/next-swc/crates/next-transform-font/src/font_imports_generator.rs](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next-swc/crates/next-transform-font/src/font_imports_generator.rs#L197)

The function tries to convert a JS object to JSON. However, the `match` expression handles only one case where the prop is plain a identifier.

I think that you should consider supporting the case where the prop is a [string literal](https://github.com/swc-project/swc/blob/main/crates/swc_ecma_ast/src/prop.rs#L102). Please note that this assumption is based on a first look. I didn't do a deep dive into how swc and next interoperate. In the meantime, we adjusted our linter settings.

### Expected Behavior

I think that using quotes around object properties in this case should compile without errors. I think string literals should not be an issue in the JS object to JSON conversion.

```ts
const inter = Inter({ 'subsets': 'latin' });
```

### To Reproduce

- Change the line [`subsets: ['latin']`](https://github.com/myl7/next-missing-font-subsets-mre/blob/f8b395881b67921e6f47e724d1cadf833e39a932/app/layout.tsx#L7) to `subsets: ['chinese-simplified']`

### Describe the Bug

`@next/font/google` fetches from Google Fonts to get the font metadata (in advance and included in the distribution) so that it can download needed fonts when building to serve them locally after deployed (correct me if wrong).

But to decide which subsets should be loaded, `@next/font/google` get the information that which subset is the WOFF file for [from the comments](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/3c84b3ac99e143cec08181616ec89d393e8dbf41/packages/font/src/google/find-font-files-in-css.ts#L16) in the Google Fonts CSS.
It is only true for some fonts like [Noto Sans Osage](https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Noto+Sans+Osage&display=swap) but not for others like [Noto Serif SC](https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Noto+Serif+SC&display=swap).
For the latter one, the comments in the Google Fonts CSS are in the form like `[4]`, `[5]` to indicate the Unicode range, other than a subset name.
That causes [the generated metadata file](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/3c84b3ac99e143cec08181616ec89d393e8dbf41/packages/font/src/google/font-data.json#L9157) to contain fonts with incorrect subsets, mostly `["latin"]` which I think is the default value.

It does not seem to avoid loading the font completely, but instead seems to load all subsets of the fonts (not so sure). However, while still working, the name of "latin" should still be confusing.

### Expected Behavior

Perfect solution: Get the correct subset information from somewhere as the metadata file included in the package.
But other than the comments, I have not found it anywhere that contains the information.

Alternatively, an additional default value can be added to indicate that the font can only be fully loaded, other than the current "latin".

prompt:
Memory leak from retained sandbox timeouts causes stepwise heap growth

### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/berry95/next-timeout-resource-leak-repro

### To Reproduce

1. Clone the reproduction repository.
2. Install dependencies with `pnpm install`.
3. Build the standalone server with `pnpm build`.
4. Start the standalone server with `pnpm start:standalone`.
5. In another terminal, run `pnpm load`.
6. Observe the reported server heap usage over repeated requests.

The reproduction sends requests to `/api/heap?timeouts=500`. The Pages Router
`middleware.ts` schedules one-shot `setTimeout(() => {}, 0)` callbacks before
the request reaches the API route. The timeout ids are not retained by user code
and `clearTimeout()` is not called, matching common fire-and-forget timeout
usage.

The `timeouts` query parameter intentionally amplifies the issue so retained
sandbox timeout resources are easier to observe locally.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

Current behavior:

Naturally completed one-shot timeouts are cleared at the underlying Node timer
level, but their numeric ids remain tracked by Next.js's sandbox
`TimeoutsManager`. The ids are removed only if user code explicitly calls
`clearTimeout(id)`, or when the whole sandbox module context is cleared.

In a long-lived standalone/self-hosted server process, repeated middleware
requests can therefore make the tracked timeout resources grow monotonically.
The production symptom is step-like heap growth over time and, under sustained
traffic, possible OOM.

Expected behavior:

After a one-shot timeout callback runs, the timeout id should be released from
Next.js's sandbox resource manager even when user code does not explicitly call
`clearTimeout(id)`.

### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System:
  Platform: win32
  Arch: x64
  Version: Windows
Binaries:
  Node: 24.14.1
  npm: 11.11.0
  pnpm: 10.33.0
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.3.0-canary.50
  react: 19.2.7
  react-dom: 19.2.7
  typescript: 5.9.3
Next.js Config:
  output: standalone
```

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)



### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

next build (local), Other (Deployed)

### Additional context

The sandbox resource managers were introduced in #57235 to avoid retaining old
Edge runtime VM contexts during dev HMR by taking ownership of timers and
clearing them when a module context is invalidated. That teardown path is still
needed.

The missing path is natural completion while the module context remains alive:
one-shot timeout callbacks can finish successfully without releasing their ids
from the sandbox manager.

The existing `clearTimeout(timeout)` inside `webSetTimeoutPolyfill` works around
the Node.js primitive timer leak described in nodejs/node#53335, but it does not
remove the id from Next.js's own resource manager.

| Scenario | RSS | Idle CPU | Disk `.next/dev/cache/turbopack` |

- Persistent turbopack cache should not grow unbounded without pruning (#81161 — @sokra acknowledged pruning is not implemented)

All tests: single heavy App Router page, 5× `curl` after cold compile, then 90 s idle.

| Config | Idle baseline (60 s) | Post-compile RSS | +90 s idle CPU |

- I am happy to capture `NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING=turbo-tasks` on a bloated `.next/dev` if useful (@sokra's request in #81161)

Under severe memory pressure, unrelated processes on my machine crash (Cursor `SIGKILL`, `core.node` from bun workers). This is collateral damage, not the root cause, but it makes the issue P0 for local development on a 32 GB machine.

getItemsLru size accounting omits URL key length, causing excessive heap retention in long-lived servers

### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/dmchoi77/nextjs-getitemslru-key-length-repro

### To Reproduce

The reproduction contains a minimal App Router app with one dynamic route handler at `/api/logs/[id]`. The included `test-memory-leak.mjs` script sends many unique long URL paths to that route. On affected versions, `getItemsLru` records one filesystem route cache entry per original URL path, but its size accounting does not include the URL key length retained by each `LRUNode`.

1. Clone the reproduction repository and install dependencies.
2. Run `npm run build` and `npm start`.
3. In another terminal, run `NEXT_LRU_REPRO_REQUESTS=1200000 node test-memory-leak.mjs`.
4. Observe the `next start` process heap over the run.
5. Take a heap snapshot of the `next start` process. `LRUNode` instances accumulate up to roughly 1,048,576 entries; each retained node holds its URL path key string plus node overhead.

The same pattern applies to production apps on `15.5.11` or later, including current canary as of 2026-06-11. The `if (!value) return 1` fix from #89040 must be present, because this report is about the residual issue that survives that fix.

Production shape where this is easiest to observe:

1. Run a long-lived self-hosted server, such as AWS ECS, a VM, or another deployment where the process uptime is measured in days rather than minutes.
2. Generate traffic with a large number of unique dynamic-route URLs, especially long URL paths such as i18n template detail paths with long percent-encoded slugs or bot-crawled URLs with varied tails.
3. Observe `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` or `runtime.node.mem.heap_used` over multiple days.
4. Take a heap snapshot. `LRUNode` instances accumulate up to roughly 1,048,576 entries; each retained node holds its URL path key string plus node overhead.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Current behavior**

In current canary as of 2026-06-11 and the latest npm release I checked that day (`next@16.2.9`), `getItemsLru` in `packages/next/src/server/lib/router-utils/filesystem.ts` is constructed with `maxSize = 1024 * 1024` and a size function shaped as `length(value)`.

That function returns:

- `1` for null negative-cache entries
- `(value.fsPath || '').length + value.itemPath.length + value.type.length` for positive entries

The URL path key, which is often the dominant memory cost per entry, is not counted in the LRU size accounting.

The current `LRUCache` implementation in `packages/next/src/server/lib/lru-cache.ts` also only calls the size function with the value:

```ts
const size = this.calculateSize?.(value) ?? 1
```

This means the cache can report tiny sizes while retaining much larger key strings:

| Quantity | Reported `size` | Actual retained cost per entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Negative cache entry, `set(itemKey, null)` | `1` | key string + `LRUNode` overhead |
| Positive cache entry | roughly `30-100` | key string + value strings + `LRUNode` overhead |

Under traffic with many unique long URL paths, the cache can grow toward its 1,048,576-entry cap. At that ceiling, a single LRU instance can retain hundreds of MB of heap even though the configured `maxSize` is nominally `1024 * 1024`.

**Expected behavior**

`maxSize = 1024 * 1024` should include the dominant per-entry string cost, matching the v14 key-aware size approximation before the custom `LRUCache` migration. In that version, the cache size function received `(value, key)` and included key length:

```js
length(value, key) {
  if (!value) return key?.length || 0
  return (
    (key || '').length +
    (value.fsPath || '').length +
    value.itemPath.length +
    value.type.length
  )
}
```

The current custom `LRUCache` should pass `key` to `calculateSize`, and `getItemsLru` should include the key length in its size calculation.

### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System: Linux (Docker, AWS ECS Fargate)
Binaries:
  Node: 22.x
Relevant Packages:
  next: 15.5.12 / 15.5.18 reproduce in production
  current canary as of 2026-06-11 and next@16.2.9 still have the same key-accounting behavior
  react: 19.x
Deployment:
  Self-hosted, long-lived containers with uptime measured in days
```

I also checked the public sources before opening this issue:

- Current canary as of 2026-06-11 still has `LRUCache.calculateSize` shaped as `(value) => number`.
- Current canary as of 2026-06-11 still calls `this.calculateSize?.(value)` in `LRUCache.set`.
- Current canary as of 2026-06-11 still constructs `getItemsLru` with `function length(value)` and does not include the URL key length.
- The latest npm release I checked, `next@16.2.9`, has the same compiled behavior.

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

- Dynamic Routes

- Route Handlers
- Runtime

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

- next start (local)
- Other (Deployed)

### Additional context

This was observed in production on a long-running self-hosted Next.js 15.5.x deployment with 3 ECS tasks and no restarts over the observation window.

Short-lived or serverless deployments may not observe this before instance recycling. The primary affected shape is a long-lived self-hosted `next start` process that sees a high number of unique dynamic-route URLs.

7-day trend:

| Metric | Day 0 | Day 7 | Delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `runtime.node.mem.heap_used` avg | 291 MB | 445 MB | +154 MB |
| `runtime.node.mem.heap_used` max | 304 MB | 470 MB | +166 MB |
| `runtime.node.mem.external` | 37 MB | 40 MB | flat |
| `runtime.node.process.uptime` | 12,327 s | 612,150 s | no restart |

Key observations:

- External memory was flat, so growth was in V8 heap rather than native memory.
- Major GC ran frequently, but retained objects survived GC.
- All 3 hosts showed similar monotonic heap growth.
- Heap growth matched accumulation of unique route-cache keys rather than total request volume.

The top retainer path in a Datadog Continuous Profiler A-to-B comparison pointed at:

```text
resolveRoutes
  -> handleRoute
    -> getItem (filesystem.ts)
      -> set (lru-cache.ts)
```

Other URL-related allocations appeared in profiles but were reclaimed by GC in local reproduction. The `lru-cache.set` path was the one producing surviving `LRUNode` instances.

#### Root cause

The key contribution to size accounting appears to have been dropped during the migration from the bundled `lru-cache` library to the self-built implementation. The old size function received `(value, key)`, while the new custom `LRUCache` stores the key on `LRUNode` but only passes `value` into `calculateSize`.

PR #89040 fixed the unbounded `size = 0` negative-cache case by making null entries return `1`, but it did not restore key-aware size accounting. As a result, the cache is now bounded by entry count for negative-cache entries rather than by the retained memory represented by those entries.

Related context:

- #71455 introduced the custom `LRUCache` migration where the key-aware `length(value, key)` behavior appears to have been dropped.
- #82633 later rewrote the custom LRU as a doubly-linked list while preserving the `calculateSize(value)` shape.
- #89033 reported the original size-0 unbounded growth.
- #89040 fixed the size-0 case by requiring positive sizes and making null filesystem cache entries return `1`, but did not restore key-aware size accounting.

#### Suggested fix

Restore key-aware size accounting by passing `key` through the `LRUCache.set` -> `calculateSize` chain:

```diff
// packages/next/src/server/lib/lru-cache.ts
- private readonly calculateSize: ((value: T) => number) | undefined
+ private readonly calculateSize: ((value: T, key: string) => number) | undefined

...

- calculateSize?: (value: T) => number,
+ calculateSize?: (value: T, key: string) => number,

...

- const size = this.calculateSize?.(value) ?? 1
+ const size = this.calculateSize?.(value, key) ?? 1
```

Then include the key length in `getItemsLru`:

```diff
// packages/next/src/server/lib/router-utils/filesystem.ts
- function length(value) {
+ function length(value, key) {
+   const keyLen = key.length
    if (!value) {
      // Null entries (negative cache) still need a non-zero size for LRU eviction
-     return 1
+     return keyLen || 1
    }
    return (
+     keyLen +
      (value.fsPath || '').length +
      value.itemPath.length +
      value.type.length
    )
  }
```

Existing one-argument `calculateSize` callbacks should continue to work with the wider callback signature.

Under traffic with many unique long URL paths, the cache can grow toward its 1,048,576-entry cap. At that ceiling, a single LRU instance can retain hundreds of MB of heap even though the configured `maxSize` is nominally `1024 * 1024`.

**Expected behavior**

`maxSize = 1024 * 1024` should include the dominant per-entry string cost, matching the v14 key-aware size approximation before the custom `LRUCache` migration. In that version, the cache size function received `(value, key)` and included key length:

```js
length(value, key) {
  if (!value) return key?.length || 0
  return (
    (key || '').length +
    (value.fsPath || '').length +
    value.itemPath.length +
    value.type.length
  )
}
```

The current custom `LRUCache` should pass `key` to `calculateSize`, and `getItemsLru` should include the key length in its size calculation.

### Provide environment information

```bash

Binaries:
  Node: 22.x
Relevant Packages:
  next: 15.5.12 / 15.5.18 reproduce in production
  current canary as of 2026-06-11 and next@16.2.9 still have the same key-accounting behavior
  react: 19.x
Deployment:
  Self-hosted, long-lived containers with uptime measured in days
```

I also checked the public sources before opening this issue:

- Current canary as of 2026-06-11 still has `LRUCache.calculateSize` shaped as `(value) => number`.
- Current canary as of 2026-06-11 still calls `this.calculateSize?.(value)` in `LRUCache.set`.
- Current canary as of 2026-06-11 still constructs `getItemsLru` with `function length(value)` and does not include the URL key length.
- The latest npm release I checked, `next@16.2.9`, has the same compiled behavior.

### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

- Dynamic Routes

- Route Handlers
- Runtime

### Which stage(s) are affected? (Select all that apply)

- next start (local)
- Other (Deployed)

### Additional context

This was observed in production on a long-running self-hosted Next.js 15.5.x deployment with 3 ECS tasks and no restarts over the observation window.

Short-lived or serverless deployments may not observe this before instance recycling. The primary affected shape is a long-lived self-hosted `next start` process that sees a high number of unique dynamic-route URLs.

7-day trend:

| Metric | Day 0 | Day 7 | Delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `runtime.node.mem.heap_used` avg | 291 MB | 445 MB | +154 MB |
| `runtime.node.mem.heap_used` max | 304 MB | 470 MB | +166 MB |
| `runtime.node.mem.external` | 37 MB | 40 MB | flat |
| `runtime.node.process.uptime` | 12,327 s | 612,150 s | no restart |

Key observations:

- External memory was flat, so growth was in V8 heap rather than native memory.
- Major GC ran frequently, but retained objects survived GC.
- All 3 hosts showed similar monotonic heap growth.
- Heap growth matched accumulation of unique route-cache keys rather than total request volume.

The top retainer path in a Datadog Continuous Profiler A-to-B comparison pointed at:

```text
resolveRoutes
  -> handleRoute
    -> getItem (filesystem.ts)
      -> set (lru-cache.ts)
```

Other URL-related allocations appeared in profiles but were reclaimed by GC in local reproduction. The `lru-cache.set` path was the one producing surviving `LRUNode` instances.

#### Root cause

The key contribution to size accounting appears to have been dropped during the migration from the bundled `lru-cache` library to the self-built implementation. The old size function received `(value, key)`, while the new custom `LRUCache` stores the key on `LRUNode` but only passes `value` into `calculateSize`.

PR #89040 fixed the unbounded `size = 0` negative-cache case by making null entries return `1`, but it did not restore key-aware size accounting. As a result, the cache is now bounded by entry count for negative-cache entries rather than by the retained memory represented by those entries.

Related context:

- #71455 introduced the custom `LRUCache` migration where the key-aware `length(value, key)` behavior appears to have been dropped.
- #82633 later rewrote the custom LRU as a doubly-linked list while preserving the `calculateSize(value)` shape.
- #89033 reported the original size-0 unbounded growth.
- #89040 fixed the size-0 case by requiring positive sizes and making null filesystem cache entries return `1`, but did not restore key-aware size accounting.

#### Suggested fix

Restore key-aware size accounting by passing `key` through the `LRUCache.set` -> `calculateSize` chain:

```diff
// packages/next/src/server/lib/lru-cache.ts
- private readonly calculateSize: ((value: T) => number) | undefined
+ private readonly calculateSize: ((value: T, key: string) => number) | undefined

...

- calculateSize?: (value: T) => number,
+ calculateSize?: (value: T, key: string) => number,

...

- const size = this.calculateSize?.(value) ?? 1
+ const size = this.calculateSize?.(value, key) ?? 1
```

Then include the key length in `getItemsLru`:

```diff
// packages/next/src/server/lib/router-utils/filesystem.ts
- function length(value) {
+ function length(value, key) {
+   const keyLen = key.length
    if (!value) {
      // Null entries (negative cache) still need a non-zero size for LRU eviction
-     return 1
+     return keyLen || 1
    }
    return (
+     keyLen +
      (value.fsPath || '').length +
      value.itemPath.length +
      value.type.length
    )
  }
```

Existing one-argument `calculateSize` callbacks should continue to work with the wider callback signature.

6. Wait 2+ minutes, re-run vmmap — **nothing is freed**

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Current**: The `@next/swc-darwin-arm64` native binary allocates IOAccelerator (MAP_JIT) memory regions during Turbopack compilation that grow monotonically and are never freed. A 5-page app with standard SaaS dependencies (better-auth, drizzle-orm, AWS SDK, chart.js, ag-charts, AI SDKs) reaches 3.5 GB of permanent IOAccelerator allocations. ### Key findings

**The SWC binary is the source** (isolated with controls):

| Process | IOAccelerator |
|---------|--------------|
| Bare Node.js | 0 MB |
| Node.js + `require(next-swc.node)` | 136 MB + 896 MB reserved |
| Next.js dev (after compiling 5 pages) | 3,500 MB |

**Not runtime-specific**: Tested with both Node.js and Bun — identical results. The allocations come from the native SWC binary, not the JavaScript runtime.

**Never freed**: After compilation completes, IOAccelerator regions persist for the lifetime of the process. Tested with 120+ seconds of idle — zero bytes reclaimed.

On Apple Silicon, IOAccelerator memory competes with GPU, media engine, and system processes for the same unified physical RAM. A developer running `next dev` on a 16 GB MacBook with a moderately-sized app can lose 8-14 GB to non-reclaimable allocations they can't see, control, or limit.

### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/Git-I985/next-head-image-empty-cache

## Description

When making a HEAD request to an image served via the Next.js Image Optimizer (/_next/image) before the image is cached, the server returns 400 Bad Request.

- **On Next.js 15.3.x:**
  - A first HEAD request poisoned the cache by storing an empty file, causing subsequent GET requests to return an empty response.
- **On Next.js 15.5.x:**
  - The cache poisoning seems fixed (no empty files are written). 
  - However, the first uncached HEAD request still fails with 400 Bad Request. 
  - Only after a GET request succeeds and the image is cached, subsequent HEAD requests return 200 OK.

This behavior breaks CDNs/proxies that issue HEAD requests for validation or preflight, since they receive a 400 instead of headers describing the resource.

### To Reproduce

**Current version**

2. Clear cache
```bash
rm -rf .next/cache/images
```
